title: Pudding Lane to Gravesend Bay: the Englishman Who Drew the Greensward
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The City of London and the Articled Years

stops.name: Pudding Lane, the surgeon's son is born
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested by the National Park Service biography. The Pudding Lane address is tradition, carried by the NYC Municipal Archives birthday post; no primary record of the house was located and the dossier itself flags it as reconstruction.
stops.campa: A son is born to Calvert Bowyer Vaux, a medical practitioner of the City of London, in the crowded parish streets above the river where the fish market and the counting houses share a wall. The family tradition puts the house on Pudding Lane, the short street where the fire of 1666 began; no primary record of it has been found. He will spend his first twenty-five years inside this square mile of brick and soot and river fog, and the remaining forty-five laying out open ground for people who have never had any. The boy is given his father's name.
sources: National Park Service, 'Calvert Vaux', nps.gov/people/calvert-vaux.htm
NYC Municipal Archives, 'Happy Birthday Calvert Vaux', archives.nyc
suggested_refs: The parish streets of Pudding Lane and Gracechurch Street, City of London

stops.name: St Benet Gracechurch, the baptism that became a birthday
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia citing the parish record. The dossier had cited this to the National Park Service page, which was fetched in full and contains only the birth and death dates; that citation is withdrawn here. Coordinate corrected roughly 110 m east of the dossier value.
stops.campa: Six weeks after the birth the infant is carried to St Benet Gracechurch and baptized. The parish date travels badly. Reprinted secondhand and then again, it detaches from the register and becomes a birthday. The National Park Service biography, which carries his name on the federal roll, records the birth and the death and nothing else, and does not mention the parish. Vaux now has two nativities in circulation, December and February, and reference works print whichever one they inherited.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Calvert Vaux', citing the St Benet Gracechurch parish record
National Park Service, 'Calvert Vaux' (checked and negative on this point)
suggested_refs: The register of St Benet Gracechurch, City of London

stops.name: Merchant Taylors' School, Suffolk Lane
stops.date_confidence: Attendance is reconstruction, from Rybczynski's 1998 essay rather than a school register; Vaux appears nowhere in the published Old Merchant Taylors list. The site is correct for the period: the school held the Suffolk Lane ground from 1561 to 1875. Date is a placeholder to order the segment.
stops.campa: The boy is schooled at Merchant Taylors' on Suffolk Lane, a classical foundation of the City, drilled in Latin and in the geometry that will later steady his drafting hand. The school has held this ground since 1561 and will not leave it until 1875. His name is in no published register of Old Merchant Taylors, and the attendance rests entirely on later biography. In 1833 his father dies and the household's circumstances narrow. What that meant for the schooling of five children, no source in reach says.
sources: Witold Rybczynski, 'Partner in the Park', New York Review of Books, 13 Aug 1998
Wikipedia, 'Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood' (site history)
suggested_refs: The Suffolk Lane and St Laurence Pountney site of Merchant Taylors' School before the 1875 removal

stops.name: Waterloo Bridge Road, articled to Cottingham
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from Kowsky on olmsted.org and Rybczynski. The widely reprinted claim that Vaux entered training at age nine is rejected by the dossier as implausible; neither that version nor the 1843 date was traced to a primary record. The contradiction is left open.
stops.campa: At nineteen he is articled to Lewis Nockalls Cottingham, a Gothic Revival architect who has spent his working life restoring medieval churches and who keeps a private museum of casts, carvings, and measured drawings taken off English cathedrals. The pupil learns the trade the way the master practises it: go to the building, measure it, draw it true, and design only after that. In this office research and design are one operation, and no primary record of Vaux's term in it survives. The museum is dispersed after Cottingham's death.
sources: Francis R. Kowsky, 'The Dual Career of Calvert Vaux', olmsted.org, 2 Jul 2024
Rybczynski, 'Partner in the Park', NYRB, 1998
suggested_refs: Cottingham's museum of architectural casts and measured drawings, dispersed after his death

stops.name: France, Belgium, and Germany, the walking tour
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, from Rybczynski by way of the dossier; not independently confirmed. Not one town on the route is named in any source in the pool, so the Brussels pin stands for the Low Countries leg only. The corpus canonical Paris pin was considered and declined: no source places Vaux in Paris.
stops.campa: With the architect George Truefitt he walks and sketches across France, Belgium, and Germany, filling books with rural scenery, gardens, and the medieval towns whose masonry he has been trained to measure. The watercolors that come home from this tour are what make him legible to a patron. He can put the picturesque on paper in an afternoon, which is a thing no amount of theory would have done for him. Not one town on the route is named in any surviving account of the journey.
sources: Rybczynski, 'Partner in the Park', NYRB, 13 Aug 1998
calvert_vaux dossier, continental tour section (tradition)
suggested_refs: Vaux's continental sketchbooks and watercolors of 1846

stops.name: Lyons Inn Hall, the Architectural Association's first meeting
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Vaux exhibited watercolors in the Association's milieu, per Rybczynski. Coordinate corrected: the dossier pinned Bedford Square, an address the Association did not occupy until 1917. In 1847 its first formal meeting was at Lyons Inn Hall off the Strand.
stops.campa: The Architectural Association holds its first formal meeting at Lyons Inn Hall off the Strand, a body founded by young draftsmen who think the articled system teaches too little and charges too much for it. It will not reach Bedford Square, the address the world now knows it by, for another seventy years. Vaux exhibits watercolors at its gatherings and attends its sketching classes. At one such evening, three years on, an American visitor hunting for a trained assistant stops in front of his drawings.
sources: Rybczynski, 'Partner in the Park', NYRB, 13 Aug 1998
Wikipedia, 'Architectural Association School of Architecture' (premises history)
suggested_refs: The Architectural Association's early exhibition and sketching-class records, 1847-1859

segments.name: The Hudson and the Downing Inheritance

stops.name: Highland Gardens, Newburgh, the partner brought back from London
stops.date_confidence: Emigration in 1850 to work with Downing at Newburgh is attested by olmsted.org citing Kowsky, and by the NPS biography. The recruitment scene, Downing seeing the exhibited watercolors and hiring on the spot, is the standard telling and is reconstruction. Month approximate.
stops.campa: Andrew Jackson Downing has crossed the Atlantic to find an architect, because America has landscape gardeners and it has carpenters and it has almost nothing in between. He comes home with a twenty-five-year-old Londoner. The valley is filling with villas built by men who have read Downing's books, and Vaux is the hand that can build what the books describe. He arrives at Highland Gardens, Downing's nursery and house above the Hudson at Newburgh, in the autumn of 1850, and within months he is named partner rather than draftsman.
sources: Francis R. Kowsky, 'The Dual Career of Calvert Vaux', olmsted.org
National Park Service, 'Calvert Vaux'
suggested_refs: Downing's Highland Gardens nursery and residence at Newburgh, since demolished

stops.name: Washington, the ground between the Capitol and the President's House
stops.date_confidence: Re-dated and upgraded. The dossier put the commission at 1851; Wikipedia has Downing commissioned in late 1850, presenting the plan to the Smithsonian Regents on 27 February 1851. Vaux's participation is independently supported by LPC report LP-2274. Range 1850-1852.
stops.campa: Downing is commissioned to lay out the public ground running from the Capitol to the President's House, and presents the plan to the Regents of the Smithsonian in February. Vaux works the commission with him, planting the grounds around the government buildings; it is the first extensive public landscape either has administered. The scheme proposes curving drives and groves where L'Enfant had drawn straight lines. Downing is dead inside eighteen months, and the plan passes to other hands. Later administrations undo what was built of it.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Andrew Jackson Downing'
NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, LP-2274, Elizabeth Home for Girls designation report
Kowsky, olmsted.org
suggested_refs: Downing's 1851 plan for the Washington public grounds, presented to the Smithsonian Regents

stops.name: The Hudson off Riverdale, the Henry Clay burns
stops.date_confidence: The event and the date are standard history; the dossier tags them reconstruction because no primary account was refetched in the verify pass, and that caution is kept. The coordinate is the accepted stretch of river near Riverdale and Yonkers. That Vaux was not aboard is uncontested in every account.
stops.campa: The steamboat Henry Clay catches fire and sinks in the Hudson off Riverdale during a race with a rival boat. Downing is aboard with his family. He drowns at thirty-six, reportedly while throwing deck chairs to people in the water. Vaux is not on the boat, and no account of the disaster places him anywhere near it. What Downing had been building, a design profession where America had none, passes at once to the surviving partner. Vaux is twenty-seven years old and has been in the country two years.
sources: calvert_vaux dossier chronology, corroborated by standard Downing biographies
Kowsky, olmsted.org
suggested_refs: Contemporary reporting of the Henry Clay disaster, 28 July 1852

stops.name: Rondout, near Kingston, the McEntee marriage
stops.date_confidence: Marriage and the McEntee kinship attested via the Smithsonian Archives of American Art finding aid for the Jervis McEntee papers, cited but not refetched; the exact date therefore reconstruction. Place given in the pool only as probably the Kingston or Newburgh area.
stops.campa: Vaux marries Mary Swan McEntee at her family's place in the Rondout country below Kingston. Her brother is Jervis McEntee, the Hudson River School painter, and the marriage sets Vaux inside the circle of artists who are at that moment teaching Americans to look at their own country as scenery worth the looking. He is an English immigrant of four years. The McEntees have been on this river for generations. The marriage will last thirty-eight years.
sources: Smithsonian Archives of American Art, Jervis McEntee papers finding aid, aaa.si.edu
suggested_refs: The Jervis McEntee papers and diaries, Archives of American Art

stops.name: Staatsburg, the house called the Point
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction left open. Wikipedia's Vaux works list gives Hoyt House, 'The Point', Staatsburg, 1855, to Vaux working independently; the dossier gives it to Vaux with Frederick Clarke Withers. Neither attribution is chosen here. Coordinate corrected by about 4 km from the dossier value, which fell off the property.
stops.campa: On the bluff at Staatsburg, Vaux designs the country house called the Point: brick and stone with a tower, set to command the reach of river below it. The house is sited to the view and the rooms are turned to take it, which is the method of every house he builds on this river. Who else worked on it is unsettled. The published works list gives the Point to Vaux alone; secondary accounts pair him on it with Frederick Clarke Withers, his partner on other Hudson Valley houses of these years. The two versions have never been reconciled.
stops.quote: The rich should study to be practical theorists, so that the less rich may be theoretical practitioners...he should be one step in advance of the rest of creation, a leader in the foremost rank of the foremost band.
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux, Villas and Cottages (1857), p. 40, seen block-quoted with page citation in a secondary study and not located in the primary OCR
sources: Wikipedia, 'Calvert Vaux', works list
William Alex and George B. Tatum, Calvert Vaux: Architect & Planner (1994), cited in the dossier project register
suggested_refs: Hoyt House standing roofless in Mills-Norrie State Park, Staatsburg

stops.name: 110 Broadway, the office in the city
stops.date_confidence: The address is attested by the letterhead of the 12 May 1865 letter in the Rotunda edition of the Olmsted Papers. The 1856 move and the naturalization year are dossier reconstruction; no primary naturalization record has been located, and the gap is stated rather than filled.
stops.campa: Vaux moves his base from the Hudson Valley down to Manhattan and takes an office at 110 Broadway with Frederick Clarke Withers. From this address, in the decade to come, he writes the letters to Frederick Law Olmsted that are the frankest surviving account of what building Central Park cost the men who designed it: the fights over credit, the forged signature under his own name. He is naturalized a citizen of the United States somewhere about this time. No primary record of the year has been located, and none of the standard biographies supplies one.
sources: Vaux to Olmsted, 12 May 1865, The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0007 (letterhead)
calvert_vaux dossier, New York practice section
suggested_refs: The Vaux & Withers letterhead, 110 Broadway, New York

stops.name: New York, Villas and Cottages published
stops.date_confidence: First Harper & Brothers edition attested; the Internet Archive scan is the 1874 reissue, Getty Research Institute copy. AIA founding membership in 1857 is attested by Wikipedia; the dossier had cited it to TCLF, whose pioneer page does not mention the AIA at all, and that citation is withdrawn here.
stops.campa: Harper and Brothers publish Villas and Cottages: A Series of Designs Prepared for Execution in the United States, a book of designs with plans and costs and an argument running under them. The argument is that good building is not a luxury owed to the rich but a thing owed to everybody, and that American villages should give up the surveyor's grid. The book goes into further editions through 1874. The same year Vaux becomes a founding member of the American Institute of Architects.
stops.quote: The great charm in the forms of natural landscape lies in its well-balanced irregularity...we want far less formality and restraint in the plans of our new villages. The roads should wind in graceful, easy curves, and be laid out in accordance with the formation of the ground and the natural features of interest.
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux, Villas and Cottages (New York: Harper & Brothers, 1857), pp. 51-52; matched against the Internet Archive OCR of the book
sources: Internet Archive, archive.org/details/villascottages00vaux (1874 Harper edition, Getty Research Institute copy)
Wikipedia, 'Calvert Vaux'
The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux
suggested_refs: Villas and Cottages, first edition 1857, further editions to 1874

stops.name: Vaux's house, Manhattan, the competition entry drawn at night
stops.date_confidence: That Vaux pressed for a competition and then partnered with Olmsted is attested by the NPS biography. That the entry was drafted at Vaux's own house, often at night, is reconstruction from Kowsky and the Central Park Conservancy's competition history; the house coordinate is approximate and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Vaux has spent two years pressing the city to throw the park design open to competition instead of letting the board's own engineer build his own scheme unopposed. When it is opened he goes to Frederick Law Olmsted, the park's superintendent, a man he barely knows, and proposes they enter together. They work at Vaux's house through the autumn, often after dark, Olmsted walking the ground by day and Vaux drawing what the walking found. Thirty-three entries are submitted. Theirs goes in under the name Greensward.
sources: National Park Service, 'Calvert Vaux'
Central Park Conservancy, 'Plans for Central Park', centralparknyc.org
Kowsky, olmsted.org
suggested_refs: The Greensward presentation drawings with their before-and-after flaps, Municipal Archives

stops.name: Central Park, the Greensward plan takes first prize
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Central Park Conservancy: 'The Greensward plan won on April 28, 1858.' Thirty-three entries, a two thousand dollar prize shared. The report itself is a joint document and does not divide authorship sentence by sentence, so the quotation is Vaux's only in the co-authored sense.
stops.campa: The Greensward plan takes first prize, two thousand dollars split between two men who had not worked together before the previous autumn. Its inventions are structural rather than decorative. Four transverse roads are sunk below the surface so that crosstown traffic crosses under the park without ever entering it, and carriage drive, bridle path, and footway are kept on separate systems so that none of the three interrupts the others. The report that goes with the drawings states the governing rule in one sentence.
stops.quote: The idea of the park itself should always be uppermost in the mind of the beholder.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park: 'Greensward' (1858)
sources: Central Park Conservancy, centralparknyc.org/articles/plans-for-central-park
Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan..., gutenberg.org/cache/epub/73830
suggested_refs: The four sunken transverse roads of the Greensward plan, still carrying crosstown traffic

stops.name: Bethesda Terrace, the one place architecture commands
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Central Park Conservancy's account of Vaux and the Terrace; built out 1859-1873, dated here to the start. The quotation is attributed to Vaux by the Conservancy, which gives no manuscript citation of its own.
stops.campa: At the formal heart of the park Vaux sets the Terrace: two stairways and an arcaded passage running under the drive to a fountain and the lake beyond, the one place in the whole design where building is permitted to take command of ground. Jacob Wrey Mould cuts the sculptural program into the sandstone, birds and fruit and the seasons, the entire calendar of the year carved along the balustrades. Asked how architecture stands to landscape here, Vaux gives the order of precedence.
stops.quote: Nature first, and 2nd & 3rd. Architecture after a while.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Calvert Vaux, quoted by the Central Park Conservancy, 'Calvert Vaux and Bethesda Terrace'
sources: Central Park Conservancy, 'Calvert Vaux's Bethesda Terrace', centralparknyc.org
suggested_refs: Mould's carved balustrades at Bethesda Terrace and Emma Stebbins's Angel of the Waters

stops.name: Bow Bridge, the drawn line over the lake
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the NYC Municipal Archives, which also records that all thirty-four Central Park bridges were designed to be unique.
stops.campa: Vaux throws a cast-iron span across the lake between Cherry Hill and the Ramble, an arch so shallow and so slight against the water that it reads as a drawn line rather than a structure. Cottingham's discipline is carried here into a public park: a bridge is not a type repeated down a catalogue, it is a specific answer to a specific crossing. Vaux draws thirty-four of them for this park, arches and spans over drives and streams and paths. The Municipal Archives records that every one was designed to be unlike every other.
sources: NYC Municipal Archives, 'Happy Birthday Calvert Vaux', archives.nyc/blog/2024/12/20/happy-birthday-calvert-vaux
suggested_refs: The thirty-four Central Park bridges and arches, no two alike

stops.name: The Dairy, the cottage on the slope
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the NYC Municipal Archives birthday post.
stops.campa: Vaux builds a Gothic cottage on the slope, a place where children brought into the park could be given fresh milk. Stone below, a timbered loggia above, the roofline pitched against the rock behind it. It is small on purpose and it is sited on purpose: the architecture in this park is meant to sharpen a sequence of landscape and then get out of the way of it. A visitor does not see the Dairy until the path turns and puts it there, under the trees, with the loggia open toward the meadow.
stops.quote: Nothing artificial should be obtruded on the view as an ultimatum of interest.
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park: 'Greensward' (1858), a jointly authored document that does not divide authorship sentence by sentence
sources: NYC Municipal Archives, 'Happy Birthday Calvert Vaux', archives.nyc
suggested_refs: The Dairy, Central Park, restored 1979 after use as a maintenance shed

segments.name: Mr. Green and the Question of the Name

stops.name: The park offices, Manhattan, eight years against the comptroller
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The fever episode, in which Vaux is said to have raved that Green's name must not be mentioned, rests on later historians and no medical record; the dossier flags it as tradition and it is carried as such. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Andrew Haswell Green, comptroller of the park board, controls every dollar spent on the ground and, increasingly, the question of whose name goes on the work. Vaux fights him for the better part of eight years over design authority. During a fever in 1862 he is said to have raved that Green's name was not to be spoken in the room. Olmsted has gone to the Sanitary Commission and then to a mining estate in California; Vaux holds the ground alone in New York and writes west, again and again, asking him to come back.
stops.quote: I called A.H.G. a p.s. and an m.p. in two different letters apparently inconsistent statements but still true.
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux to Frederick Law Olmsted, 3 June 1865, The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0012; A.H.G. is Andrew Haswell Green, and the abbreviations are left unglossed by the letter itself
sources: calvert_vaux dossier, Green conflict section (tradition)
Vaux to Olmsted correspondence, Rotunda edition of the Olmsted Papers
suggested_refs: Olmsted's 1882 pamphlet The Spoils of the Park, written out of this quarrel

stops.name: 110 Broadway, the letter of 12 May 1865
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Transcribed in the Rotunda edition of The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0007; punctuation and abbreviation as that edition renders them. The letter is private correspondence, not a public statement.
stops.campa: Vaux writes to Olmsted in California a letter with none of the reticence of the public documents. The commissioners want the two designers reduced to employees taking instructions, and he will not accept an executive committee's terms. His name has been printed under a woodcut he never authorized, signed Olmsted & Vaux, Landscape Archts, which he calls a direct forgery. The letter is private correspondence, never meant to be read outside the two of them. On the subject of the board itself he is briefer.
stops.quote: I then say in distinct terms I expected that and I don't care a damn for the Commrs
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux to Frederick Law Olmsted, 12 May 1865, The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0007
sources: The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda digital edition, rotunda.upress.virginia.edu
suggested_refs: The Vaux-Olmsted letters of May and June 1865 in the Rotunda edition

stops.name: Brooklyn, the park moved off its own ground
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission's Prospect Park designation report, LP-2558. The quotation is from the letter of 20 May 1865 in the Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0009, and is Vaux's fee proposal for the Brooklyn plan.
stops.campa: Brooklyn has bought land for a park that Flatbush Avenue cuts in half, with a reservoir sitting in the middle of what is left. Vaux tells the commissioners to move the whole thing: abandon the eastern parcel, take ground to the south and west, drop the reservoir, and the avenue stops being a problem because the park no longer straddles it. They agree. He then names his fee for drawing the plan, and he names it to Olmsted in California before he names it to Brooklyn.
stops.quote: I ask $5000 for plan & $5000 per ann to commence at once and expenses to Europe this summer.
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux to Frederick Law Olmsted, 20 May 1865, The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0009
sources: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, Prospect Park designation report, LP-2558
The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition
suggested_refs: The abandoned eastern parcel of the original Brooklyn park site, north of Flatbush Avenue

stops.name: The Long Meadow, Prospect Park
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Prospect Park designation report; built out 1866-1873 and dated here to the start. Coordinate corrected: the dossier value lay about 800 m south of the meadow, near the Bandshell and Parade Ground end of the park.
stops.campa: The meadow runs nearly a mile through the northern and western part of the park, unbroken, with no path crossing it in view, so that a walker standing at one end cannot see where it ends. Vaux and Olmsted are working here on ground not yet gridded, with a free hand over the whole site and no comptroller counting the stone at their backs. Neither man had that in Manhattan. What they lay out is the largest continuous open lawn in any American park, ninety acres of it.
stops.quote: If when I return in the Fall you should happen to be here again disengaged and willing to devote a decade to Landscape art, why, there is the half of Brooklyn to begin on...
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux to Frederick Law Olmsted, 20 May 1865, The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted, Rotunda edition, OLMS-print-01-05-02-0012-0009
sources: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, Prospect Park designation report, LP-2558
Wikipedia, 'Prospect Park (Brooklyn)'
suggested_refs: The Long Meadow, Prospect Park, ninety acres of unbroken lawn

stops.name: Delaware Park, Buffalo, a city planned as a system
stops.date_confidence: The Olmsted and Vaux authorship of the Buffalo park and parkway system is attested by TCLF; the exact 1868 start is reconstruction, corroborated only in general terms. Kowsky's 2013 book on the system is cited through the dossier and was not fetched.
stops.campa: In Buffalo the firm proposes something no American city has yet had: not a park but a system. Three large grounds at different edges of the city, joined to each other and to the street plan by broad planted parkways, so that the park stops being a destination and becomes a condition of the whole town. Delaware Park sits at the middle of it, meadow and lake. Buffalo takes the plan and builds it. Kowsky's study of what resulted is called The Best Planned City in the World.
sources: The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux
Francis R. Kowsky, The Best Planned City in the World: Olmsted, Vaux, and the Buffalo Park System (2013), cited in the dossier
suggested_refs: The Buffalo park and parkway system: Delaware, Cazenovia, and Martin Luther King Jr. parks with their connecting parkways

stops.name: Riverside, Illinois, curves against the section grid
stops.date_confidence: Re-dated to a range. Wikipedia gives Riverside as designed in 1869 by Vaux and Olmsted; the firm was engaged in 1868 and the General Plan is dated 1869. The dossier's flat 1868 is a year early for the plan and a year late for the engagement.
stops.campa: Nine miles west of Chicago, on flat prairie broken only by the Des Plaines River, the firm lays out a suburb of curving roads that follow the river terrace and refuse the section grid coming at them from every direction. Houses are set back thirty feet. The common ground along the water is kept open to everyone. The railway station anchors the plan and the roads bend toward it. The curves are copied for the next century by developers who keep neither the river nor the commons. The firm was engaged in 1868; the General Plan is dated 1869.
sources: The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux
Wikipedia, 'Riverside, Illinois'
Olmsted, Vaux & Company, General Plan of Riverside (1869)
suggested_refs: The 1869 General Plan of Riverside, Illinois, and its accompanying report

stops.name: Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, a park that is a road
stops.date_confidence: Attested through the Prospect Park designation report; the dossier dates the work only to the 1870s and the year here orders the segment.
stops.campa: Vaux and Olmsted carry the park out past its own boundary and into the street: a wide central drive with planted malls and service roads either side, running east from Prospect Park through Brooklyn land not yet built on. They call it a parkway and they mean the word literally. A city's green ground ought to be continuous rather than parcelled out, and a man ought to be able to leave his own door and reach the park without ever leaving the planting. Nothing of the kind has been built in the United States before. The trees go into ground where there are as yet no houses.
sources: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, Prospect Park designation report, LP-2558
calvert_vaux dossier, chronological section
suggested_refs: Eastern Parkway, Brooklyn, among the first parkways built in the United States

stops.name: Olana, Hudson, consulted at the outset
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the dossier overstated the source. Bergdoll's essay on olana.org gives no dates at all and says only that Olana was created in consultation at the outset with Vaux; at the outset points earlier than 1870, since Church bought the land in 1860. Coordinate corrected about 690 m west onto the hill.
stops.campa: Frederic Edwin Church has bought the hill across the river from Catskill and means to build on it. Vaux is consulted at the outset. What survives of the contribution is a set of principles rather than a set of drawings: window openings, bay windows, and porches treated as devices for framing a view, which is the doctrine of Villas and Cottages, a book Church owned. The Persian towers and the stencilled ornament are Church's own synthesis, worked out with a painter's eye. No source gives a date for Vaux's advice.
sources: Barry Bergdoll, essay on Olana, olana.org/barrybergdoll/
Calvert Vaux, Villas and Cottages (1857)
suggested_refs: Olana, Frederic Edwin Church's house above the Hudson at Greenport

stops.name: New York, the firm wound up
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a date by olmsted.org's Kowsky-based timeline: '1872: Olmsted-Vaux partnership ended.' No source in the pool gives a reason for the dissolution, and none is supplied here.
stops.campa: Olmsted, Vaux and Company is wound up after seven years. The two men will work together again, at Niagara and on the memorial park at Newburgh, but never again as a firm. The division of temperament was always in the partnership: Olmsted an administrator and a writer who thought in policy, Vaux an architect who thought in built fabric, and between them a running argument about which of the two the public had been told designed Central Park. Whether any of that ended the firm, no document either man left says.
sources: Olmsted Network, olmsted.org, Kowsky timeline
The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux

stops.name: Parliament Hill, Ottawa, grounds for another country's capital
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The only sustained study is J. J. Stewart's 1976 article on the 1873 design, cited through the dossier and not fetched; it sits behind a JSTOR paywall. How much of the scheme was executed is not established by anything reachable.
stops.campa: Canada asks Vaux for the grounds around its new Parliament buildings, on the cliff above the Ottawa River. He supplies a design in 1873. It is carried out in part and modified afterward by other hands. The only sustained study of the scheme is an article published a century after the fact, written from the drawings rather than from the site and held behind a paywall. What of the design still stands on the cliff cannot now be separated from what came later.
sources: J. J. Stewart, 'Notes on Calvert Vaux's 1873 Design for the Public Grounds of the Parliament Buildings' (1976), JSTOR 1493555, cited in the dossier, not fetched
suggested_refs: Vaux's 1873 drawings for the Parliament Hill public grounds, Ottawa

stops.name: Jefferson Market, Greenwich Village, the courthouse and the lookout tower
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Village Preservation, which also carries the poll of American architects. Built 1874-1877.
stops.campa: With Frederick Clarke Withers, Vaux builds a courthouse at the crossing of Sixth Avenue and Tenth Street: red brick and granite, steep gables, stained glass, and a clock tower doubling as a fire lookout, a High Victorian Gothic pile dropped whole into the middle of Greenwich Village. Nothing about it is quiet. In a poll of American architects taken the following decade it comes fifth on the list of the ten most beautiful buildings in the United States.
stops.quote: if excellent architecture can give innocent pleasure, it is certainly worth having, and all Americans ought to have it...simply because it is worth having
stops.quote_source: Calvert Vaux, Villas and Cottages (1857), p. 41, seen block-quoted with page citation in a secondary study and not located in the primary OCR
sources: Village Preservation, 'Calvert Vaux and the Village', villagepreservation.org/2018/12/20/calvert-vaux-and-the-village/
suggested_refs: The Jefferson Market Courthouse, now a branch of the New York Public Library

stops.name: Riverside Park and Drive, the Hudson bluff
stops.date_confidence: Vaux's involvement is attested; the phasing is reconstruction from the dossier project register and NYC Parks records. Two separate phases, 1873-1875 and again in the 1880s, and no single fetched source separates the hands at work.
stops.campa: Along the Hudson bluff above Seventy-second Street, Vaux works on a park and a drive that have to run four miles down a slope too steep to level, with a railroad at the foot of it. He works the job in two separate phases, one in the mid-1870s and another in the following decade. The authorship is genuinely tangled. Olmsted's name is on some of it and later designers on a good deal more, and no source in reach separates the hands. The park visible today is the sum of half a century of revision, with the railroad still running at the foot of the slope.
sources: calvert_vaux dossier project register
NYC Department of Public Parks records, cited in the dossier
suggested_refs: Riverside Park and Riverside Drive, Manhattan, authorship shared across fifty years

stops.name: Manhattan Square, the first museum of natural history
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction: AMNH Research Library records are cited through the dossier and were not fetched. The Ruskin relation is one-directional and intellectual, tagged R in the research pool because the verify pass could not re-fetch it; no meeting between Vaux and Ruskin is documented anywhere.
stops.campa: Vaux and Jacob Wrey Mould draw a master conception for a museum on Manhattan Square: a vast rectangle of courtyards and connected halls, of which the first Ruskinian Gothic building is all that ever gets built to their design. It opens in 1877. The manner comes from John Ruskin's books and so does the argument beneath it, that ornament should be cut by a workman who is thinking rather than stamped out by a machine. Vaux read Ruskin. There is no record the two men ever met.
sources: AMNH Research Library records, cited in the dossier
NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, on the Ruskinian Gothic character of the building
John Ruskin, The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849) and 'The Nature of Gothic', The Stones of Venice II (1853)
suggested_refs: The 1877 Vaux and Mould building, now enclosed within the American Museum of Natural History

stops.name: Central Park, the Metropolitan Museum opens
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the Metropolitan Museum's own institutional history, cited in the dossier; corroborated as a major Vaux work by TCLF, fetched directly.
stops.campa: The Metropolitan Museum's first purpose-built home opens inside Central Park on the thirtieth of March, a polychromatic Gothic building by Vaux and Mould with a high glazed hall. The trustees begin complaining about it almost at once. Within twenty years a Beaux-Arts front is going up on Fifth Avenue in front of it, and the additions keep coming until the original is entirely swallowed. The walls are still there, roofed over inside the present building. Nothing of the 1880 elevation can be seen from Fifth Avenue or from the park.
sources: Metropolitan Museum of Art, institutional history, metmuseum.org/about-the-met/history
The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux
suggested_refs: The surviving Vaux and Mould fabric of 1880, enclosed within the Metropolitan Museum of Art

stops.name: The Department of Public Parks, back on the payroll
stops.date_confidence: Attested at 1887 by both the NYC Municipal Archives and olmsted.org. The dossier carried a duplicate return dated 1881 tagged as attested; that tag was unsupported by every source fetched and the duplicate is dropped. The 1879 abolition of the landscape-architect office is reconstruction from Olmsted's 1882 pamphlet.
stops.campa: Vaux comes back into the Department of Public Parks, where he will work until he dies, under Samuel Parsons Jr., a man half his age whom he trains. His independent architectural practice has fallen away. The Gothic manner he built in has gone out of fashion, and the coming style is the classical one that will be put on show at Chicago in 1893 and will govern American public building for the next forty years. He is sixty-two. The department abolished the office of landscape architect eight years ago.
sources: NYC Municipal Archives, archives.nyc, on the 1887 return under Parsons
Olmsted Network, olmsted.org, Kowsky timeline
Frederick Law Olmsted, The Spoils of the Park (1882), cited in the dossier
suggested_refs: Samuel Parsons Jr., Vaux's pupil and successor in the Department of Public Parks

stops.name: Niagara, the plan for the State Reservation
stops.date_confidence: Attested by the NPS biography: '1887: Collaborated with Olmsted on improvements to the New York State Reservation at Niagara Falls.' The geography lens dates the work 1885-1887 and the chronology lens 1887; the plan is catalogued at the Library of Congress in the Commissioners' Supplemental Report of 1887.
stops.campa: Olmsted and Vaux, fifteen years out of partnership, write together the General Plan for the Improvement of the State Reservation at Niagara. The argument is restraint. Strip the mills and the fences and the paying stiles off the bank; restore native growth to the islands; build only enough path and shelter to let people reach the water; and do not, whatever else is done, make an ornamental park out of a cataract. Thirty years have passed since the Greensward drawings, and it is the last work the two of them do together. The plan is printed in the commissioners' supplemental report of 1887.
sources: National Park Service, 'Calvert Vaux'
Library of Congress, Supplemental Report of the Commissioners of the State Reservation at Niagara (1887), loc.gov/item/03029139/
suggested_refs: The General Plan for the Improvement of the State Reservation at Niagara, 1887

stops.name: Downing Park, Newburgh, the debt paid without a fee
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The fee waiver, the dedication to Downing, and the participation of Downing Vaux and John Charles Olmsted all come from the dossier and are consistent with olmsted.org and TCLF but were not independently fetched. The park opened in 1897.
stops.campa: Newburgh wants a park and cannot pay for a plan. Vaux and Olmsted offer the design without a fee, thirty-seven years after the Henry Clay went down, on the condition that the park carry Downing's name. Their sons work on it with them: Downing Vaux, named for the dead man, and John Charles Olmsted. It is a small park on a hill above the town where Vaux came ashore in 1850 knowing nobody and learned the trade. It opens in 1897, two years after his death.
sources: calvert_vaux dossier, chronological section
Olmsted Network project history, olmsted.org
suggested_refs: Downing Park, Newburgh, the last Olmsted and Vaux collaboration

stops.name: 307 East 12th Street, the Elizabeth Home for Girls
stops.date_confidence: Attested by LPC designation report LP-2274, fetched as PDF and read with pypdf: 'Built 1891-2, Vaux & Radford, architects.' Coordinate corrected about 280 m northwest onto the East 12th Street block between First and Second Avenues. The dossier dated the Children's Aid Society buildings from 1876; LP-2274 places them in the 1880s and 90s and dates the Radford partnership to about 1873, formalized 1876.
stops.campa: For the Children's Aid Society, Vaux and George Kent Radford put up a home for girls on East Twelfth Street: brick, ornamental banding, a stepped Dutch gable over a block of tenements. There are about twelve of these buildings, lodging houses and industrial schools, raised through the 1880s and 1890s for poor and working children, with the era's disciplinary assumptions built into them as firmly as the light and the ventilation Vaux fought for. The designation report states his intention exactly.
stops.quote: Vaux worked to evoke the imagery of a snug country inn in the middle of New York City.
stops.quote_source: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, designation report LP-2274, Children's Aid Society, Elizabeth Home for Girls
sources: NYC Landmarks Preservation Commission, LP-2274, s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2274.pdf
Olmsted Network, olmsted.org, listing twelve Children's Aid Society buildings with Radford, 1876-1893

stops.name: The Palisades near Closter, the horse bolts
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The account comes through the Library of Congress Frederick Law Olmsted Papers timeline, cited in the dossier and not refetched in the verify pass. Nothing Vaux wrote about it has been located.
stops.campa: A carriage horse bolts in the Palisades woods near Closter. Mary Vaux, thirty-eight years married to him, takes a skull fracture and lives about a week. Vaux is sixty-seven. Everyone who writes about his last three years dates the change from this afternoon: the withdrawal, the health that never comes back. The detail reaches us through a timeline compiled around Olmsted's papers rather than through anything Vaux wrote himself, and he seems to have written nothing.
sources: Library of Congress, Frederick Law Olmsted Papers timeline, loc.gov, cited in the dossier
suggested_refs: The Palisades woods above Closter, New Jersey, before the Interstate Park

stops.name: Rockwood Park, Saint John, New Brunswick
stops.date_confidence: The two research lenses disagree on this one and the disagreement is left open: the chronology lens tags it reconstruction as dossier tradition, the geography lens tags the same claim attested, citing the TCLF pioneer profile. What Vaux actually drew, and how much of it was built, is established by nothing reachable.
stops.campa: Saint John engages Vaux for a landscape plan over the rough ground of lakes and rock ledge above the harbour town, a thousand acres of granite and spruce and standing water. He is sixty-nine, a year from his death, working for a Canadian municipality with very little money. Others develop the ground after he dies. How much of what stands there is his, the record does not say, and the accounts differ even on whether the commission is firmly documented or only traditional. The engagement is among the last entries in his working life.
sources: The Cultural Landscape Foundation, tclf.org/pioneer/calvert-vaux
calvert_vaux dossier project register
suggested_refs: Rockwood Park, Saint John, New Brunswick, among the largest urban parks in Canada

stops.name: Mulberry Bend, a park cut out of the Five Points
stops.date_confidence: Attested per the dossier project register citing NYC Parks history, which was not itself fetched; the NYC Parks pages returned 403 Forbidden to the verify pass. The park opened after Vaux's death and was later renamed Columbus Park.
stops.campa: The Bend is the worst block of the old Five Points district, and the city has finally taken it, cleared the tenements off it, and handed Vaux the empty ground. He is seventy, in the last year of his life, laying out a park on the site of the slum that his generation of reformers spent thirty years describing to each other. He does not see it open; it is dedicated after his death and renamed, later still, for Columbus. What he draws is plain enough: trees, a path system, and open ground where the alleys stood.
sources: calvert_vaux dossier project register, citing NYC Parks history (parks pages returned 403 to the verify pass)
suggested_refs: Columbus Park, Manhattan, formerly Mulberry Bend Park

stops.name: Bath Beach, Brooklyn, out into the fog
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Bowery Boys History, fetched directly, drawing on contemporary New York Sun and Tribune reporting. The son's statement about his father's state the previous evening is from the same source.
stops.campa: Vaux is staying at his son's house on Twentieth Avenue in Bath Beach, out on the Brooklyn shore. He is a month short of seventy-one and still on the payroll of the Department of Public Parks. On the morning of the nineteenth he goes out into a heavy fog. He has left behind his watch, his chain, and his vest, and he is carrying about two dollars. His son will say afterward that his father had been cheerful the evening before and entirely in his right mind.
sources: Bowery Boys History, 'The Mysterious Death of Calvert Vaux', boweryboyshistory.com
suggested_refs: Calvert Bowyer Vaux's house on Twentieth Avenue, Bath Beach, Brooklyn

stops.name: A pier near Bath Beach, the last sighting
stops.date_confidence: Reduced from the dossier, which over-stated the source. Bowery Boys hedges twice: he was spotted by a 'Captain Ditmar', possibly Captain Walter Earl Ditmar, on a pier near the water. The name sits in scare quotes in the source and the full identification is the writer's conjecture. The shoreline conversation the dossier reports is not in the source at all.
stops.campa: Somewhere along the shore during the day, a man the papers call Captain Ditmar sees Vaux on a pier. That is the whole of the last sighting: a name in quotation marks in the reporting, an old man standing on the planking, fog on Gravesend Bay. It is somewhere between the morning and the dark; the hour is not given either. Whether anything was said, and what, no source records. Later accounts have supplied a conversation about improving the shoreline. The contemporary reporting does not contain one.
sources: Bowery Boys History, 'The Mysterious Death of Calvert Vaux', boweryboyshistory.com
suggested_refs: The New York Sun and New York Tribune reports of Vaux's disappearance, November 1895

stops.name: The foot of Bay 17th Street, the body found
stops.date_confidence: Re-dated. The dossier gives 21 November in three separate lenses; Bowery Boys dates the discovery to 20 November, and the 21st is the publication date of the New York Times report it links. The pool also gives two different coordinates for this site, 40.5906,-74.0009 and 40.599,-74.005; the latter is used and the disagreement is noted.
stops.campa: On the twentieth a workman on Fry's coal dock, later named as Benjamin Butler, sees a body being tossed about in the rough water at the foot of Bay Seventeenth Street. There is a bruise on the head and a slight cut over the eye; the hat, the spectacles, and the left shoe are gone. The death certificate records drowning. The press of that week entertains a suicide theory the family rejects outright, and modern retellings conclude he fainted or tripped. Nothing found on him settles it either way.
sources: Bowery Boys History, 'The Mysterious Death of Calvert Vaux', boweryboyshistory.com
Wikipedia, 'Calvert Vaux', which states accidental drowning without qualification
suggested_refs: The New York Times report of 21 November 1895 on the recovery of the body

stops.name: Montrepose Cemetery, Kingston, the McEntee plot
stops.date_confidence: Burial at Montrepose attested by Wikipedia; the McEntee-plot specification is uncited by anything fetchable. Coordinate corrected roughly 1.4 km southeast of the two different values the dossier carried. The funeral foliage detail is tradition and had been sitting under an attested tag; it is downgraded here.
stops.campa: He is buried at Montrepose Cemetery in Kingston, in his wife's family ground, three years after her. The funeral is deliberately plain. The park commissioners of New York are said to have sent, in place of cut flowers, foliage gathered out of the parks themselves, a gesture his son thought more fitting than anything a florist could have supplied; the detail runs through the biographical tradition and through no source that can be retrieved. No photograph of the marker has been located.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Calvert Vaux': 'Buried in Kingston, New York's Montrepose Cemetery'
calvert_vaux dossier, death and burial section (tradition)

stops.name: Calvert Vaux Park, the shoreline given his name
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Wikipedia, 'In 1998, the city of New York dedicated Calvert Vaux Park ... to him.' Coordinate corrected roughly 1.5 km southeast; the research pool carried three different values for this single park. The absence of any personal memorial inside Central Park is a negative finding from the Central Park Conservancy's own page and is tagged as reconstruction.
stops.campa: New York gives his name to a waterfront park on Gravesend Bay, a filled and reclaimed stretch formerly called Dreier-Offerman, ballfields and made ground on the Brooklyn shore, a short walk from where the body came ashore. There is no monument to him in Central Park and none in Prospect Park; what stands for him in both is the fabric itself, the terrace and the thirty-four bridges and the mile of unbroken meadow. The Brooklyn dedication is in 1998, a hundred and three years after the drowning.
